name: Harden the control plane and kubelets
objective: CKS › Cluster + System Hardening (15% + 15%). Drill EVERY hardening corner harder than the exam on a real multi-node kind cluster: control-plane manifest perms, kubelet read-only port + anonymous-auth + authz mode, two apiserver admission/flag hardenings, least-privilege RBAC, ServiceAccount token hardening, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Harden control-plane manifest file permissions
questions.teach:
Static pod manifests under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` carry sensitive flags, so CIS wants them mode `0600` (`rw-------`) and owned `root:root`. On a kind cluster each node is a container, so operate via `docker exec $CP ...` and verify with `stat -c '%a %U:%G'`.

**Gotcha:** changing a manifest's mode/owner does NOT restart its pod (safe live) — only editing its *contents* does.
questions.prompt:
The kube-scheduler static pod manifest on control-plane `$CP` was left world/group readable at mode `644`. Set `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` to exactly mode `600`, owned `root:root`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` prints `600 root:root`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root
questions.eli5:
Picture the control-plane node as a server room, and inside it a set of blueprints (**static pod manifests**) that describe how the cluster's core services start up. Those blueprints list sensitive details, so the security checklist (CIS) says two things about each one: only the owner may open it (**mode `600`**, i.e. `rw-------`), and the owner must be the building superintendent (**`root:root`**).

Someone left the kube-scheduler blueprint at mode `644` — meaning the group and the whole world could read it. Your job is to lock it back down to `600` and confirm it's owned `root:root`.

On a **kind** cluster there's a twist: each "node" is really a Docker container, not a separate machine. So you don't SSH in — you step inside the node with `docker exec $CP ...`, then run `chmod`/`chown`/`stat` there.

The reassuring part: changing a manifest's **lock or owner does not restart its pod**. The kubelet only re-launches a static pod when the blueprint's *contents* change. Tightening permissions is pure metadata, so the running kube-scheduler never blinks — a safe, live fix.

**Watch out for:**

- **Two things to satisfy: mode `600` AND owner `root:root`.** A `600` file owned by someone else still fails the owner check.
- **`stat` shows `600`, not `0600`** — the leading zero is just hidden.
- **`640`/`644`/`660` all leak** to the group or world — only `600` (or stricter like `400`) passes.
- **chmod/chown do NOT restart the pod** — only editing the blueprint's *contents* does. No downtime here.
- **Control-plane node only** — use `docker exec $CP`, not a worker container.
questions.deepDive:
## Hardening control-plane manifest file permissions — full rundown

### Mental model
Static pod manifests in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` tell the kubelet how to launch the control-plane pods and embed sensitive flags. CIS section **1.1** requires each manifest at mode `0600` (`rw-------`) **and** owned `root:root`. Both conditions must hold. On **kind**, every node is a Docker container, so you operate with `docker exec $CP` instead of SSH. Permission/owner changes are metadata-only, so the pod does **not** restart.

### Unix permissions refresher
Octal mode = **owner / group / other**, each digit = read(4)+write(2)+execute(1).

| Mode | Symbolic | owner | group | other | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `600` | `rw-------` | rw | — | — | ✅ |
| `400` | `r--------` | r | — | — | ✅ (stricter) |
| `640` | `rw-r-----` | rw | r | — | ❌ group read |
| `644` | `rw-r--r--` | rw | r | r | ❌ world read |
| `660` | `rw-rw----` | rw | rw | — | ❌ group write |

`stat -c '%a'` prints octal without the leading zero → `600`.

### CIS manifest controls (section 1.1)
| Files | Mode control | Owner control |
|---|---|---|
| `kube-apiserver.yaml`, `kube-controller-manager.yaml`, `kube-scheduler.yaml`, `etcd.yaml` | `600` or stricter | `root:root` |

### The fix (kind, control plane `$CP`)
```bash
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
# -> 600 root:root

# harden all four at once:
docker exec $CP sh -c 'chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml && chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml'
```

### Why metadata changes are restart-free
The kubelet watches these files and re-creates a static pod only when the **content** (hash/mtime of the body) changes. `chmod`/`chown` touch permission bits/ownership, not content, so the running pod is untouched. Editing the manifest **body** (flags) *does* restart it — that's the contrast with later apiserver steps.

### kind vs real clusters
| | kind | kubeadm bare-metal/VM |
|---|---|---|
| Reach the node | `docker exec $CP ...` | `ssh node` |
| Manifest path | `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` | same |
| Commands | identical `chmod`/`chown`/`stat` | identical |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Both mode AND owner.** A `600` file owned by a non-root user still FAILs the owner check — set `root:root`.
- **`stat` drops the leading zero** — expect `600`, not `0600`.
- **Only `≤600` passes.** `640`/`644`/`660` leak to group/world.
- **No restart from chmod/chown** — don't delete/recreate the pod; metadata changes are live-safe.
- **Right node.** Manifests live on the **control plane** (`$CP`); `docker exec $W1` finds nothing.
- **Glob needs a shell** inside `docker exec`: wrap in `sh -c '...'`.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root
```
Rule: **manifests → `600 root:root`.**

questions.title: Disable the kubelet read-only port
questions.teach:
The kubelet **read-only port** (`10255`) serves pod/node metadata with no auth and no TLS. CIS requires it off: set `readOnlyPort: 0` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `systemctl restart kubelet`. Any non-zero value leaves it enabled.

**Gotcha:** the edit does nothing until the kubelet restarts, and the node goes `NotReady` briefly — wait ~20s and confirm it's `Ready` again. If it stays `NotReady`, a bad edit kept the kubelet down: `docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail` names the error (🧰 Node toolbox).
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W1` the kubelet is serving its read-only port (seeded as `readOnlyPort: 10255`). Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W1` so `readOnlyPort: 0`, then restart the kubelet and give the node ~20s to report `Ready` again.

Target: the config on `$W1` has `readOnlyPort: 0` AND node `$W1` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: node $W1 is still Ready after the kubelet restart

questions.eli5:
Every worker node runs a kubelet, and the kubelet can leave a little **unlocked mail slot** open called the read-only port (`10255`). Anyone who can reach the node can stick their hand in and pull out a live list of the pods and node info — no password, no encryption. It's an information leak, like leaving a copy of the building's floor plan taped to the outside door.

The hardening rule is simple: **seal the slot** by setting `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet's config file, `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`. Zero means "closed."

But sealing it on paper isn't enough. The kubelet read its config when it first woke up and won't notice your edit until it wakes up again — so you have to **restart the kubelet** (`systemctl restart kubelet`). On kind, both the edit and the restart happen inside the worker container with `docker exec $W1`.

When the kubelet restarts, the node briefly shows `NotReady` while it reconnects — that's normal. Wait about 20 seconds and it flips back to `Ready`.

**Watch out for:**

- **The edit does nothing until you restart the kubelet** — forget the restart and the slot stays open.
- **A bad edit can keep the kubelet from starting**, leaving the node stuck `NotReady`. If it doesn't recover after ~20s, check `docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail` — it names the error (the Node toolbox).
- **It must be exactly `0`.** Any other value leaves the port enabled.
- **A brief `NotReady` right after the restart is expected** — give it ~20s before worrying.
- **This is a worker-node fix** (`$W1`), done via `docker exec`.
questions.deepDive:
## Disabling the kubelet read-only port — full rundown

### Mental model
The kubelet can expose port `10255` as an **unauthenticated, unencrypted** read-only API serving pod/node metadata and metrics. Anyone with network reach to the node can scrape it — a reconnaissance leak with no credentials required. Hardening = set `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet's `KubeletConfiguration` and restart the kubelet so it re-reads config.

### The setting
```yaml
# /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
readOnlyPort: 0        # 0 = disabled; any non-zero (e.g. 10255) = enabled
```
`readOnlyPort` is a **top-level** key, not nested under `authentication`/`authorization`.

### The fix (kind, worker `$W1`)
```bash
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1       # wait ~15-20s for Ready
```

### Edit vs apply: why the restart
The kubelet parses `config.yaml` **only at process start**. Editing the file changes nothing in the running process until `systemctl restart kubelet`. This is a **content** change (unlike a `chmod`, which is metadata and needs no restart).

| Change | Restart kubelet? |
|---|---|
| `chmod 600 config.yaml` (perms) | No |
| `readOnlyPort: 0` (content) | **Yes** |

### Node NotReady recovery
A kubelet restart drops the node to `NotReady` for ~15-20s while it re-registers — expected. If it **stays** NotReady, the edit broke config and the kubelet won't start:
```bash
docker exec $W1 systemctl status kubelet --no-pager
docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail -n 40
# typical: "failed to load Kubelet config file" / YAML parse error / unknown field
```
Fix the YAML, restart again, wait.

### Verifying the port is gone
```bash
# from inside the node, the port should no longer listen:
docker exec $W1 sh -c 'ss -lntp | grep 10255 || echo "10255 closed"'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No restart → still enabled.** The most common miss: editing the file but leaving the old kubelet process running.
- **Exactly `0`.** `10255` or any other value keeps it open.
- **Top-level key.** Don't mistakenly nest `readOnlyPort` under another block.
- **Brief NotReady is normal;** only act if it doesn't recover in ~20s — then read `journalctl -u kubelet`.
- **Worker node.** This is a per-node kubelet setting (`$W1`), not the control plane.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1          # Ready after ~20s
# troubleshoot: docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail
```

questions.title: Lock down kubelet authn/authz
questions.teach:
An unprotected kubelet lets anyone hit its API. CIS requires `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false` and `authorization.mode: Webhook` (not blanket `AlwaysAllow`) in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then a kubelet restart.

**Gotcha:** `anonymous.enabled` is nested under `authentication:` and `mode` under `authorization:` — edit the right blocks, not stray top-level keys. After the restart, if `$W2` stays `NotReady`, a malformed `config.yaml` stopped the kubelet — `docker exec $W2 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager` shows the parse error (🧰 Node toolbox).
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W2` the kubelet was seeded insecure: `authentication.anonymous.enabled: true` and `authorization.mode: AlwaysAllow`. Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W2` so anonymous auth is **disabled** and the authorization mode is **Webhook**, then restart the kubelet and let `$W2` go `Ready` again.

Target: on `$W2`, `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false` AND `authorization.mode: Webhook`, and node `$W2` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: In `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W2`, set the `enabled:` under `authentication.anonymous` to `false` and the `mode:` under `authorization` to `Webhook`; then `docker exec $W2 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W2 sed -i 's/^\(\s*enabled:\).*/\1 false/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # under authentication.anonymous
docker exec $W2 sed -i 's/^\(\s*mode:\).*/\1 Webhook/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml       # under authorization
docker exec $W2 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W2   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: kubelet on $W2: anonymous auth false + authorization mode Webhook, node Ready

questions.eli5:
The kubelet runs its own little API on each node. Two questions decide who gets to use it: **"Who are you?"** (authentication) and **"What are you allowed to do?"** (authorization). If both are left wide open, any stranger on the network can boss the kubelet around — read logs, exec into containers, the works.

Two switches in the kubelet's config file (`/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`) fix this:

- **`authentication.anonymous.enabled: false`** — "Don't accept nameless visitors." With it `true`, requests with no identity are treated as a built-in anonymous user; turning it `false` means you must prove who you are.
- **`authorization.mode: Webhook`** — "Ask the apiserver whether this identity is actually allowed." The insecure default `AlwaysAllow` just says *yes* to everyone; `Webhook` delegates the decision to the cluster's real permission system.

The fiddly part is **where** these live. They're nested: `enabled` sits *inside* `authentication:` → `anonymous:`, and `mode` sits *inside* `authorization:`. You must edit those specific nested keys, not invent new top-level ones. After editing, restart the kubelet so it re-reads the file.

**Watch out for:**

- **Mind the nesting.** `enabled:` belongs under `authentication.anonymous`, `mode:` under `authorization`. A stray top-level `enabled:` or `mode:` does nothing (or breaks the file).
- **You MUST restart the kubelet** (`systemctl restart kubelet`) — the edit alone changes nothing.
- **A malformed `config.yaml` stops the kubelet**, leaving `$W2` stuck `NotReady`. If it doesn't recover in ~20s: `docker exec $W2 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager` shows the parse error (the Node toolbox).
- **Values are case-sensitive**: it's `Webhook` (capital W), not `webhook`, and boolean `false`, not the string `"false"` where YAML expects a bool.
- **Worker node `$W2`**, via `docker exec`.
questions.deepDive:
## Locking down kubelet authn/authz — full rundown

### Mental model
The kubelet serves an HTTPS API (port `10250`) used for logs, exec, metrics, and pod spec. Two config blocks gate it:
- **Authentication** — *who are you?* By default `anonymous.enabled: true` admits unauthenticated callers as `system:anonymous`.
- **Authorization** — *what may you do?* `mode: AlwaysAllow` approves everything. Secure clusters use `mode: Webhook`, which asks the apiserver's `SubjectAccessReview` whether the caller is permitted.

CIS requires `anonymous.enabled: false` **and** `authorization.mode: Webhook`. Both are in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`; apply with a kubelet restart.

### The config shape (note the nesting)
```yaml
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false          # CIS: disable anonymous auth
  webhook:
    enabled: true           # (typically already true)
  x509:
    clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
authorization:
  mode: Webhook             # CIS: NOT AlwaysAllow
```

### The two controls
| Control | Key (path) | Insecure value | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anonymous auth | `authentication.anonymous.enabled` | `true` | `false` |
| Authz mode | `authorization.mode` | `AlwaysAllow` | `Webhook` |

### Authorization modes
| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `AlwaysAllow` | Approves every request — **insecure** |
| `Webhook` | Delegates each decision to the apiserver (SubjectAccessReview) — **CIS-compliant** |
| `AlwaysDeny` | Denies all (not usable) |

### The fix (kind, worker `$W2`)
```bash
# the two keys are indented; match the nested lines
docker exec $W2 sed -i 's/^\(\s*enabled:\).*/\1 false/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # under authentication.anonymous
docker exec $W2 sed -i 's/^\(\s*mode:\).*/\1 Webhook/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml     # under authorization
docker exec $W2 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W2       # wait ~15-20s for Ready
```
> The `sed` above is blunt (matches the first `enabled:`/`mode:`). In the lab the seeded file has a single relevant `enabled:` and `mode:`; on a richer config, edit the exact nested keys (e.g. with a YAML-aware edit) to avoid hitting `webhook.enabled`.

### Why a restart
These are **content** changes to the kubelet config; the kubelet only re-parses config at startup. Edit → `systemctl restart kubelet` → node briefly `NotReady` (~15-20s) → `Ready`.

### When $W2 stays NotReady
A malformed config (bad indentation, string vs bool, typo) stops the kubelet:
```bash
docker exec $W2 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail -n 40
# e.g. "cannot unmarshal string into Go value of type bool" (quoted "false")
# or "unknown field" (key at wrong nesting level)
docker exec $W2 systemctl status kubelet --no-pager
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Nesting is everything.** `enabled` lives under `authentication.anonymous`; `mode` under `authorization`. A top-level `enabled:`/`mode:` is ignored or rejected.
- **Case-sensitive values.** `Webhook` (capital W), not `webhook`. `false` as a YAML boolean, not `"false"`.
- **Don't flip the wrong `enabled:`.** `authentication.webhook.enabled` should stay `true`; only `anonymous.enabled` goes `false`.
- **Must restart the kubelet** — edit alone does nothing.
- **Brief NotReady is normal;** persistent NotReady → read `journalctl -u kubelet`.
- **Worker node (`$W2`).**

### Quick reference
```bash
# authentication.anonymous.enabled: false   +   authorization.mode: Webhook
docker exec $W2 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W2          # Ready after ~20s
docker exec $W2 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail   # if NotReady
```

questions.title: Re-enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin
questions.teach:
`NodeRestriction` is an apiserver **admission controller** limiting each kubelet to modifying only its own Node and the Pods bound to it. Enable it in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` via `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...` — one flag, comma-separated.

**Gotcha:** saving the manifest auto-restarts the apiserver; a typo takes it DOWN — wait ~20–60s for it to come back.
questions.prompt:
Setup removed `NodeRestriction` from the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins`. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP` so the flag includes `NodeRestriction` again (keep any other plugins), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `NodeRestriction` in `--enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $CP sed -i '/- kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` (or append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value). Wait ~20s for the restart.
questions.solution:
# Setup removed the flag line, so add it back under the kube-apiserver args:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# (If the flag already exists with other plugins, instead append ,NodeRestriction to its value.)
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
questions.eli5:
Each worker node's kubelet has a staff badge that lets it talk to the cluster's brain (the apiserver). Left unchecked, a kubelet could use that badge to meddle with *other* nodes and *other* pods — so if one node gets compromised, the attacker can spread. Too much power for a single node.

**NodeRestriction** is a rule that clips the badge down to size. It's an **admission controller** — a gatekeeper inside the apiserver — and its job is: "A kubelet may change only *its own* Node record and the Pods assigned to *it*, and nothing else." One hijacked node can no longer vandalize the whole cluster.

You turn the gatekeeper on by listing `NodeRestriction` in the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins` flag, inside `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml`. That flag is **one comma-separated list** — so you add `NodeRestriction` alongside any plugins already there (or re-add the whole flag if setup deleted it), never wiping out the others.

Because the apiserver is a **static pod**, just **saving the file** makes the kubelet restart it automatically — no `kubectl apply`. The trade-off: a typo takes the apiserver down for a bit, and `kubectl` goes quiet until it recovers.

**Watch out for:**

- **One comma-separated flag.** Keep existing plugins; append `,NodeRestriction`. Don't overwrite the list.
- **Saving auto-restarts the apiserver** — a mistake takes it DOWN for ~20-60s, and `kubectl` stops answering meanwhile. Edit carefully; wait for it to return.
- **No `kubectl apply`** — static pods update by the kubelet watching the file, not via the API.
- **Confirm on the running pod**, not just the file: `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins`.
- **Control-plane node only** (`$CP`), via `docker exec`.
- **Indentation matters** when you insert the flag line — misaligned YAML crash-loops the apiserver.
questions.deepDive:
## Re-enabling the NodeRestriction admission plugin — full rundown

### Mental model
Admission controllers are gatekeepers that run inside the apiserver after authn/authz, before an object is stored. **NodeRestriction** constrains requests coming from kubelet identities (`system:node:<name>`, group `system:nodes`): a kubelet may modify **only its own Node object and the Pods bound to it**. It blocks a compromised node from editing other nodes, spoofing labels, or self-escalating. Enable it in the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins` flag. The apiserver is a static pod, so saving its manifest auto-restarts it.

### The control
| Flag | Required |
|---|---|
| `--enable-admission-plugins` | must **include** `NodeRestriction` |
| `--authorization-mode` | should include `Node` (the Node authorizer that NodeRestriction complements) |

### One comma-separated list
```
--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,...
```
Preserve existing plugins. Two cases:

**A) flag present with other plugins** — append `,NodeRestriction`:
```yaml
- --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity,NodeRestriction
```
**B) flag missing (this lab)** — add the line under the command:
```bash
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
```

### Manifest context
```yaml
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction   # <- here
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
    # ...
```

### Static-pod restart behaviour
| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Save manifest | kubelet re-creates the apiserver pod automatically |
| `kubectl apply` | wrong — mirror pod is read-only; static pods aren't API-managed |
| Typo / bad flag | apiserver crash-loops; `kubectl` unreachable during the gap |

### Verify on the running pod
```bash
# wait ~20-60s after saving
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
docker exec $CP grep enable-admission-plugins /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
```

### If the apiserver won't come back
```bash
docker exec $CP crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
docker exec $CP sh -c 'crictl logs $(crictl ps -a -q --name kube-apiserver | head -1)' 2>&1 | tail
# usual cause: misaligned YAML from the sed insert, or a flag typo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Don't clobber other plugins** — it's a single list; append.
- **No `kubectl apply`** — just save the file on `$CP`.
- **Saving restarts the apiserver** → 15-60s outage; `kubectl` errors are expected.
- **Verify on the running pod**, not only the file.
- **Indentation of the inserted flag line must match** the other args, or YAML breaks and the apiserver won't start.
- **Full effect needs `--authorization-mode=Node`** too (kubeadm default).
- **Control plane only (`$CP`).**

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
```

questions.eli5:
The apiserver has a built-in "mechanic's diagnostic port" called **profiling** — the `/debug/pprof` endpoints. They dump deep internals (memory, CPU, goroutine traces) that are great for a developer debugging performance, but in production they hand an attacker a detailed x-ray of how the server works and can even be abused to stress it. The security checklist (CIS) says: in production, turn it off.

You turn it off by adding one flag to the apiserver's settings file (`/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on the control-plane node): `--profiling=false`.

Here's the subtle trap: profiling is **on by default**. So you cannot fix this by simply *not mentioning* the flag — if it's absent, the default `true` wins and you still FAIL. The flag has to be **present and explicitly set to `false`**. "Say nothing" is not the same as "say no."

Because the apiserver is a **static pod**, saving the file makes the kubelet restart it automatically. Give it ~20 seconds, then confirm the flag actually landed on the *running* pod.

**Watch out for:**

- **Omitting the flag is NOT compliant.** The default is `true`; you must explicitly add `--profiling=false`.
- **Exact spelling and value**: `--profiling=false` (lowercase `false`), one flag line among the apiserver args.
- **Saving auto-restarts the apiserver** — a typo takes it down ~20-60s and `kubectl` goes quiet; wait for it to recover. No `kubectl apply`.
- **Verify on the running pod**, not just the file: `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep -- --profiling`.
- **Indentation matters** when inserting the line, or the YAML breaks and the apiserver crash-loops.
- **Control-plane node only** (`$CP`), via `docker exec`.
questions.deepDive:
## Turning off apiserver profiling — full rundown

### Mental model
The kube-apiserver exposes Go profiling endpoints under `/debug/pprof` when `--profiling` is enabled. These leak internal runtime detail (heap, CPU, goroutines) useful to an attacker for fingerprinting and potentially as a DoS lever. CIS requires `--profiling=false` on the apiserver (and likewise on controller-manager and scheduler). Critically, **the flag defaults to `true`**, so it must be *explicitly present and set to false* — omission is non-compliant. The apiserver is a static pod; saving its manifest auto-restarts it.

### The control
| Flag | Default | Required | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--profiling` | `true` | `false` | disables `/debug/pprof` information leak |

> Same rule applies to `kube-controller-manager` (CIS 1.3.x) and `kube-scheduler` (CIS 1.4.x) manifests.

### The fix (kind, control plane `$CP`)
```bash
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --profiling=false' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# wait ~20s for the restart, then verify on the RUNNING pod:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep -- --profiling
```

### Manifest context
```yaml
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --profiling=false        # <- explicit; default would be true
    # ...other flags...
```

### Why "absent" ≠ "false"
| State of flag | Effective value | CIS verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Flag absent | `true` (default) | ❌ FAIL |
| `--profiling=true` | `true` | ❌ FAIL |
| `--profiling=false` | `false` | ✅ PASS |

This is the whole trap: many flags are safe-by-default, but `--profiling` is *insecure-by-default*, so you must set it.

### Static-pod restart behaviour
| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Save manifest | kubelet re-creates the apiserver pod |
| `kubectl apply` | wrong — static pod, not API-managed |
| Bad edit | crash-loop; `kubectl` unreachable briefly |

### If the apiserver won't come back
```bash
docker exec $CP crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
docker exec $CP sh -c 'crictl logs $(crictl ps -a -q --name kube-apiserver | head -1)' 2>&1 | tail
# usual cause: YAML indentation off, or flag typo (e.g. --profile=false)
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Omitting the flag FAILs** — default is `true`; add `--profiling=false` explicitly.
- **Exact value `false`** (lowercase); it's `--profiling`, not `--profile`.
- **One flag line** among the args, correctly indented — misalignment breaks the manifest.
- **Saving auto-restarts** the apiserver (~20-60s outage); no `kubectl apply`.
- **Verify on the running pod**, not just the file.
- **Control plane only (`$CP`).**
- Don't forget the sibling controls exist for controller-manager/scheduler if an exam task says "harden the control plane components".

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --profiling=false' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep -- --profiling   # --profiling=false
```
